title: Foreign secy Misri discusses ‘multifaceted’ ties with Nepal foreign minister, expected to call on PM Balen - ThePrint
description: Foreign secy Misri discusses ‘multifaceted’ ties with Nepal foreign minister, expected to call on PM Balen  ThePrint
publisher.title: ThePrint
full_article:
In his meeting with Khanal, Misri “discussed prospects for expanding” the “multifaceted” relationship between the two countries. Misri is on a two-day visit to the Himalayan country at the invitation of Foreign Secretary Rai. The Indian Foreign Secretary is expected to call on Shah before departing for New Delhi.

“The bilateral talks covered the entire gamut of Nepal-India relations, including exchange of high-level visits, connectivity, trade, development cooperation, energy and people to people relations, underscoring the strong bond between the two countries,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Nepal said in a statement on the Misri-Rai meeting.

Misri also met Nepal’s Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal and Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha.

Misri is on a two-day visit to Nepal on 4 and 5 November. He is expected to depart Kathmandu for New Delhi Thursday. Apart from meeting high-level officials, the Foreign Secretary is expected to finalise the agenda for Shah’s visit.

The new Prime Minister of Nepal is expected to make his first official bilateral visit to India. He had earlier attended the United Nations General Assembly in September, where he spoke on the cost of climate change and its impact on Nepal following the glacial flood, which occurred in the country at the end of August.

For Nepal, its key areas of interest with India remain the production of clean-energy, greater border connectivity and other infrastructure projects. Misri was expected to visit Nepal earlier in May, however, the visit fell through due to a number of factors, including Shah’s reluctance to meet with officials who are not of equivalent level.

Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle made a visit to India in September to discuss reconstruction of the country following the glacial flood and bilateral ties. It was considered as an important opening to further stabilise ties between the two neighbouring countries.

Earlier this year, Nepal was miffed over the route of the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage which included travellers travelling through the pass at Lipulekh, which Kathmandu claims as a part of its territory. India had rejected Nepal’s claims, pointing that this route has been in use since at least the 1950s.

Foreign Minister Khanal had visited India in June and met with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar. In comments to ThePrint at the time, Khanal underlined that Kathmandu is looking to solve the border dispute “bilaterally”. Shah had reached out to the UK and China for documents relating to Lipulekh earlier this year.

India has publicly confirmed that it has invited Shah to visit India, which has been pending for almost half a year now. Shah was elected as Prime Minister in March. The previous Nepal government led by K.P. Oli resigned in September 2025 following the youth protests across the country.

title: “Nepal Must Turn Climate Commitments into Action” - Khabarhub
description: “Nepal Must Turn Climate Commitments into Action”  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
The impacts and risks of climate change are intensifying in Nepal. Recent disasters, particularly the incidents in the Gandaki region and the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, have sent a strong message to the international community that Nepal is among the countries highly vulnerable to climate change. The Prime Minister also highlighted several critical climate-related concerns at the recent United Nations General Assembly.

Although Nepal has formulated various policies, programmes and roadmaps to address climate change, translating these commitments into action remains a major challenge. Adequate financial resources, along with strong political will and administrative and institutional commitment, are essential to ensure their effective implementation.

According to the preliminary assessment of the Bhotekoshi floods, the Government of Nepal has estimated the cost of damage recovery at approximately USD 723 million. However, this figure does not account for indirect economic losses, trade-related costs or the full value of damage to natural resources. Therefore, the actual cost is likely to be considerably higher.

So far, Nepal has managed to secure approximately USD 930 million through around 30 climate-related projects at various stages of implementation. This indicates the need to improve the effectiveness of project preparation and adopt a more strategic approach to accessing climate finance. We should learn from countries such as China, which have successfully mobilised substantial financial resources through large-scale, strategically designed projects.

Ultimately, Nepal’s challenge is not simply to secure more climate finance, but to ensure that available resources are effectively mobilised and translated into tangible outcomes.

At present, considerable financial pressure remains in the areas of infrastructure reconstruction and community rehabilitation. Community rehabilitation, in particular, is a complex process that requires careful planning and assessment. Nepal should draw important lessons from its post-earthquake recovery experience to develop more effective approaches.

Several private-sector banks and institutions have also started taking initiatives in this area. Government-affiliated and supervised institutions, including the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) and the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC), are also contributing, alongside international organisations such as the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). However, a fundamental question remains: do our institutions have the necessary capacity to access, manage and effectively implement these financial resources?

Nepal must move beyond the identity of a climate-vulnerable nation and position itself as a proactive leader in climate action. To achieve this, several key priorities need to be addressed.

First, Nepal should strengthen regional cooperation with neighbouring countries, particularly China and India, in areas such as data sharing, joint research and development, and the establishment of technical standards for climate-resilient infrastructure. The mountain agenda and regional coordination should also be promoted through South-South cooperation platforms rather than relying solely on individual representation at global forums.

Second, Nepal must strengthen its international presence and climate-related claims through credible evidence, reliable data and comprehensive statistics, in accordance with the protocols and requirements governing access to the Loss and Damage Fund.

Third, the implementation of existing climate projects must be accelerated. Although Nepal has secured financial resources for various initiatives, progress on the ground remains slow. Strengthening institutional and technical capacity is essential to ensure that allocated budgets and programmes are effectively delivered to communities at the grassroots level.

The existing project-design and financing mechanisms also need substantial improvement. Under the current system, where much of the process is concentrated within the Ministry of Finance, coordination gaps have emerged between technical ministries and the actual needs of local communities. Although climate-finance guidelines emphasise the importance of directing a substantial share of resources towards communities, the proportion reaching provincial and local governments remains limited.

It is therefore misleading to assume that climate finance has reached communities simply because the relevant expenditure has been recorded under specific budget codes. What matters is whether the resources have actually reached the intended beneficiaries and produced meaningful results. This requires a stronger focus on institutional capacity development, effective coordination and transparent financial delivery mechanisms.

As Nepal prepares for COP31, it must give greater prominence to the mountain agenda, evidence-based documentation of climate-related losses and damages, and the broader concept of coordination from the mountains to the sea. These issues should be firmly incorporated into Nepal’s national statements and negotiating priorities.

Nepal must further strengthen its presence, voice and priorities in international climate diplomacy. Equally important is the need to consolidate fragmented institutional structures, equip them with adequate resources and technical expertise, and establish stronger climate governance mechanisms. Effective coordination among federal, provincial and local governments must also be institutionalised at the policy and implementation levels.

Ultimately, Nepal’s challenge is not simply to secure more climate finance, but to ensure that available resources are effectively mobilised and translated into tangible outcomes. Moving from climate vulnerability to climate leadership will require strong institutions, evidence-based diplomacy, regional cooperation and, above all, the capacity to turn commitments into action.

title: Helicopters collide near Mount Everest, killing 1, Nepal Police say - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: Helicopters collide near Mount Everest, killing 1, Nepal Police say  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
Two helicopters crashed into each other as they attempted to land near Mount Everest in Nepal on Tuesday, killing one person and injuring three others, including both pilots, according to the Nepal Police.

A man stands next to a damaged helicopter after two helicopters collided as they prepared to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region November 3, 2026. Nepal Police via Reuters

The helicopters crashed at a helipad in the Solukhumbu district, police said. The crash was caught on a livestream weather camera run by Webcam Nepal after about 8 a.m. local time.

Both helicopters were attempting to land at the helipad in Pheriche, which sits at an altitude of about 4,200 meters and is on the way to an Everest base camp, Nabin Raja Budhathoki, the deputy superintendent of police and the head of the office in Solukhumbhu, told ABC News.

A pilot was the only passenger onboard one of the helicopters, which was a commercial cargo craft operated by Air Dynasty, police said. That helicopter was flying from Lukla to Pheriche.

The other, which was operated by Fishtail Air, was returning from an Everest base camp carrying a pilot and two foreign passengers, one of whom died at the scene, police said.

A helicopter is seen in Solukhumbhu, a district in Nepal, after two craft collided on Nov. 3, 2026, in an image supplied by the Nepal Police Solukhumbhu. Nepal Police Solukhumbhu

The man who died at the scene was identified as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu, of Chennai, India, police said. The other passenger was Shailesh Krishan Patel, of New Zealand, police said, adding that Patel was seriously injured and was airlifted directly to Nepal Mediciti Hospital in Kathmandu.

The crash may mark another setback for Nepal’s vital tourism and aviation sectors.

title: Why Nepal are missing from the SAFF Championship 2026 - The Daily Star
description: Why Nepal are missing from the SAFF Championship 2026  The Daily Star
publisher.title: The Daily Star
full_article:
As the SAFF Championship 2026 kicks off in Dhaka on Thursday, the regional footballing fraternity will notice a glaring omission.

Nepal, traditionally one of South Asia's most passionate footballing nations, are entirely missing from the tournament bracket. This marks an unprecedented omission for the Himalayan nation who have never won the competition. Nepal have reached the final once, in 2021, but suffered a 3-0 defeat to India.

Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source

The absence has nothing to do with sporting merit, but rather a severe administrative crisis that has completely isolated the country from the international game.

Read more SAFF Championship around the corner, but no one seems ready

On June 24, world football's governing body, FIFA, handed a blanket suspension to the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA), citing third-party government and administrative interference in the federation's operations.

The suspension was the culmination of an escalating domestic crisis in Kathmandu. Nepal's Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) and other government bodies had launched aggressive probes into ANFA's financial dealings. Investigations surrounding jersey sales, ticketing irregularities, and murky administrative practices crossed FIFA's strict statutory red lines, which mandate that member federations must manage their affairs independently and without legal or political interference from their governments.

Despite the active ban, the South Asian Football Federation (SAFF) initially attempted to throw Nepal a lifeline. During the official tournament draw ceremony on August 1, organisers granted ANFA a two-month grace period to settle its internal disputes.

While Nepal were naturally excluded from the initial draw pots, SAFF declared that if the federation could appease FIFA and have the suspension lifted by September 30, the team would be parachuted directly into the group featuring host nation Bangladesh.

That two-month window came and went without a resolution. With the September 30 deadline officially missed, the door was firmly shut on Nepal's participation in the 15th edition of the regional showpiece.

The fallout extends far beyond just the SAFF Championship. Under the ongoing FIFA and Asian Football Confederation (AFC) sanctions, Nepal's national teams and domestic clubs remain strictly barred from all official international competitions.

title: UAE in good place for Nepal clash after beating Oman for third successive win - The National
description: UAE in good place for Nepal clash after beating Oman for third successive win  The National
publisher.title: The National
full_article:
Basil Hameed says the UAE will head to Nepal for next month’s World Cup Qualifier Play-off full of confidence after claiming a third consecutive victory.

The national team cruised to a 42-run win over Oman at the ICC Academy in the final match of Cricket World Cup League Two. It was their third win in a tri-series also involving the Netherlands.

Even though it was not enough to lift them from last-place in the eight-team league, the successes provided a morale boost before the assignment in Kathmandu.

Abu Dhabi T10: Everything you need to know about revamped 2026 tournament Read More Arrow

The play-off – which will also involve Nepal, Namibia, Canada, Jersey, Kuwait, Italy and Uganda – is the last chance to advance to the final phase of World Cup qualifying. That is the global qualifier in Namibia and South Africa in February and March.

More pertinently, though, the UAE’s one-day international status – plus the large tranche of ICC funding which comes with it – will also be at stake in Nepal.

Basil was the player of the match against Oman after making a quick-fire 43 to help hoist the hosts to 226-8 from their 50 overs.

During Oman’s run chase, he then took two fine catches – even though he was only returning to the side after suffering an injury while doing exactly that on his previous outing in the series.

He also took a wicket as Oman were restricted to 184-9 in the chase, and he said momentum is with the UAE as they prepare to head to Kathmandu.

“This will definitely add some confidence,” Basil said. “We’ve been unlucky to have some losses, especially when we scored 330 against USA [in a tri-series in Dallas last month].

“We could have cashed in and won that match, which could have brought us even more momentum into these games.

“But we are happy to be on a winning side, winning three on the trot, so we'll definitely take some good confidence for the qualifiers.”

Capping the series with a match award also represented a positive personal return for Basil.

The 34-year-old all-rounder had been out of the UAE’s ODI side for the best part of two years before he was recalled for the trip to Dallas.

“I've been putting in the hard yards behind the scenes, having faced some injuries recently as well,” Basil said.

“As a senior pro, people expect a little more from, especially when you have played more than 100 matches [55 ODIs and 65 T20Is]. So, there is baggage behind you.

“I was taking away all those things. I just wanted to contribute in any aspect of the game, irrespective of which number I bat.

“I will happily do whatever team requires at that stage. Alhamdulillah, I did it in a very strong manner, I believe.”

His all-round effort was commendable given he could hardly grip the ball when he bowls, because of the effects of his hand injury.

“When you play cricket, I always believe that if you have three aspects of the game, you make more chances as a player,” he said.

“I've always been working on the fielding and bowling, irrespective of what outcome it was, if I get to bowl or not.

“I've always stood up with my bowling in domestic matches. Obviously, I love batting the most, but it doesn't matter; in international cricket you cannot wish for your spot.

full_article:
NEW DELHI: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah is expected to visit India later this month on his first bilateral foreign trip since assuming office in March 2026, Nepal foreign secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said on Wednesday.

The visit is likely to take place in the last week of November, possibly between November 23 and 25, although the dates have not been officially announced. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri, who is on a two-day visit to Kathmandu, held talks with Rai on Wednesday to prepare the groundwork for the visit. Rai described Misri's visit as instrumental in laying the groundwork for Shah's trip to New Delhi. The two foreign secretaries discussed bilateral cooperation in connectivity, trade, energy, development projects and people-to-people relations. Misri also met Nepal's finance minister Swarnim Wagle to discuss economic cooperation. Shah is expected to seek India's financial assistance for reconstruction following devastating flash floods in Nepal. Connectivity, trade and infrastructure development are also likely to figure prominently in the discussions. He is also expected to address a business conclave in New Delhi. Referring to the damage caused by flooding in the Bhotekoshi region, Misri said India and Nepal had stood by each other in difficult times. He said India had already extended assistance and stood ready to consider further requests for reconstruction and rehabilitation projects. "We have extended assistance but we recognise that this incident has caused enormous damage and destruction to the infrastructure of Nepal," Misri said. A Nepal foreign ministry statement said the talks covered the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and underscored the strong ties between the two neighbours.

A New Zealand man who was injured in a deadly helicopter crash in Nepal is recovering in a Kathmandu hospital and says it's "sheer luck" he survived.

The New Zealand Herald spoke to West Auckland man Shailesh Krishan Patel, 53, from his hospital bed.

While Patel suffered only minor injuries in the crash, an Indian tourist was killed after two choppers collided as they prepared to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region.

Patel told the Herald he was returning from Everest Base Camp when the crash happened - saying trekking to the camp had been a bucket-list goal.

Mt Everest Base Camp. (File photo) 123rf

After reaching Base Camp with three others guided by Pristine Nepal Treks, Patel and another member of the group boarded a helicopter for the return journey.

He told the Herald the crash happened "before we could blink our eyes".

"We had no chance to hold anything.

"The impact I think was more on the side where my friend was sitting and I think he had some really bad head injury."

The helicopters were operated by two private firms, Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air. Fishtail Air said in a statement that its helicopter was carrying passengers who had been rescued from the Everest region when it crashed while landing.

A Dynasty Air official said its helicopter was carrying only cargo.

Patel was recovering in hospital where he was treated for bruising and discomfort in his legs.

He told the Herald his wife and son were in New Zealand and he'd spoke to them following the crash.

"They were happy to hear me."

Patel said he was grateful to be alive and he hoped to return home soon after he had recovered.

"Definitely, I was lucky ... my friend was sitting just next to me on my right-hand side and I was really lucky, just sheer luck."

The accident happened during the peak trekking season in Nepal, when helicopters ferry hikers and climbers in the region.

Small helicopters are widely used in the Himalayan nation to transport tourists, climbers and supplies, as well as to carry out emergency evacuations.

title: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

full_article:
Serious flash flooding in Nepal on Wednesday morning has left over a hundred reported dead and hundreds more missing, including at least 47 American tourists, Nepali officials said, after a massive wall of water tore through a region on the Nepal-Tibet border.

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district, along the border with Tibet, at around 8:40 a.m. local time on Wednesday, authorities said, inundating coastal areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

In a statement, Nepal's office of the prime minister expressed "deep sorrow" over the loss of life. "Offering heartfelt tribute to all those who lost their lives in this natural disaster, it extends its sincere condolences to the bereaved families and relatives," the statement shared on social media said.

Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Related Deadly Nepal flood caused by enormous landslide, glacier tumble: Scientist

The prime minister's office later said search and rescue operations carried out by the Nepali Army would continue through the night.

Nepali police said 162 were killed in the flood-affected areas, while Chinese state-run media Xinhua News Agency reported three dead. Authorities said the identification process is ongoing.

A resident walks along a street covered in mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devghat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, August 26, 2026. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

At least 403 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali tourists are reported missing, according to the Prime Minister's Office of Nepal. Chinese media reported 265 missing.

The Nepali Tourism Board reported that the missing includes at least 47 American tourists who have been out of contact since floods hit the Rasuwa region.

The State Department said the number of Americans among the missing and otherwise impacted by the floods has fluctuated throughout the day, and that officials don’t yet have an accurate figure.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 27, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

"The United States extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the devastating flash floods in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster," a department spokesperson said in a statement issued later Wednesday.

The spokesperson said the State Department is "closely monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts. The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities."

Houses lie partially submerged in muddy water along a riverside after flash floods at Trishuli Bazar in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. A massive flood swept through Nepal's northern Rasuwa district on August 26, damaging roads and power infrastructure as authorities scrambled to assess the scale of the destruction. Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty Images

An influential Indian spiritual guru and entrepreneur known as Sadhguru said in a post on social media that 77 people who were on tours organized by his Isha Foundation were at an immigration center at the Nepal-Tibet border when the floodwaters came rushing in. Isha Foundation has confirmed to ABC News that 22 of the 77 people are Americans.

Rescuers gather on a rooftop as floodwaters sweep through Trishuli Bazar following a flash flood, in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Narendra Shrestha/EPA/Shutterstock

Many of them were traveling to or from Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak near the border between Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China. Mount Kailash, which is part of a Hindu pilgrimage called the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, is revered by many Hindus as the spiritual home of the god Shiva.

The Isha Foundation, which is headquartered in India, also has a base in McMinnville, Tennessee. The group's coordinator told ABC News the group has been in touch with family members in the U.S.

Three of the missing Americans were listed as traveling with a Nepali company called Fishtail Tours and Travel. The agency confirmed to ABC News that three American nationals are among the missing tourists traveling with them.

A drove view of mud covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

Efforts to locate and rescue the missing tourists are ongoing, the company said, without providing any further information on their possible whereabouts or well-being.

The Nepal Tourism Board said that local tourism and law enforcement authorities were "working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists and travelers who were in or traveling through the affected areas."

Nepali authorities have mobilized 656 police personnel to respond as of 7:30 p.m. local time, according to police.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Reuters

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 20 kilometers northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China border, according to Nepal Disaster Management.

A 5.2-magnitude landslide impacted Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The seismic activity from the landslide was initially erroneously reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, the agency said. It is unclear what triggered the landslide.

A geophysicist at New York's Columbia University told ABC News it appeared a landslide in the Himalayas took away a large glacier or parts of a glacier in the mountain pass.

The U.S. Embassy in Kathmandu said in posts to X that it was "deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life and devastation" caused by the flooding. "We are closely tracking developments and remain in close contact with Nepali authorities," the embassy said.

Also among the foreign nationals listed as missing in the Tourism Board's preliminary count were Indian, Malaysian, British, South African, Dutch and Australian tourists.

A boy looks at the devastation caused by flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Three army helicopters attempted to fly in to conduct relief operations Wednesday but had to turn back due to bad weather between Kathmandu, Nepal and the flooded areas, Sunil Sharma, spokesperson at Nepal Tourism Board, told ABC News.

Authorities are working to identify victims and conduct rescue efforts, and they hope rescue flights can resume tomorrow if the weather improves, Sharma said.

title: Nepal’s Supreme Court Orders Cannabis Regulation: Could Adult Use Be Next? - High Times Magazine
description: Nepal’s Supreme Court Orders Cannabis Regulation: Could Adult Use Be Next?  High Times Magazine

full_article:
Switch to Dark Mode

Nepal’s Supreme Court has given the government three months to establish a framework for cannabis cultivation and production for medical, scientific, and industrial purposes. The ruling also opens the door to discussions about potentially reforming the country’s recreational cannabis laws. Fifty years after the 1976 restrictions, the Himalayan nation is once again facing a question that cuts across its history, economy, and traditions: What role should the plant play in Nepali society?

Contents Nepal and Cannabis—Before and After Prohibition

Medical Cannabis Was Already Allowed in Nepal, but Never Regulated

Could Nepal Legalize Adult-Use Cannabis?

Cannabis in Ayurveda

Nepal has three months to fulfill a legal obligation that has gone unmet for nearly half a century. The country’s Supreme Court has ordered the government to establish the regulations needed to oversee cannabis cultivation and production for medical, scientific, and industrial purposes, after finding that authorities had failed for decades to fulfill their legal obligation to implement the regulatory framework already provided for under existing law, according to a report by ABC .

The ruling, whose full text was made public in late October, stems from a petition filed by attorney Saroj Adhikari and other petitioners seeking a review of the country’s cannabis restrictions and the creation of a legal framework for the plant’s cultivation and use.

But the court’s decision goes beyond medical marijuana. Although it did not order the legalization of adult use, the country’s highest court also urged authorities to consult with experts and explore possible reforms to the existing prohibition.

The decision carries particular historical weight in Nepal, a country that became one of the world’s most iconic cannabis culture destinations during the 1960s, before tightening its laws in 1976 amid mounting international pressure.

Then legal hashish-shop in Kathmandu (1973). Roger McLassus., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Nepal and Cannabis—Before and After Prohibition

Kathmandu became famous around the world as a major destination along the legendary Hippie Trail. During the 1960s and 1970s, thousands of backpackers, Western travelers, and artists, including figures such as George Harrison and Jimi Hendrix, made their way to Jhochhen Tole, a street in the capital that eventually earned the nickname Freak Street .

In Nepal, hashish and marijuana were completely legal and sold under government-issued licenses, under regulations adopted in 1961 and 1962. Among the establishments operating in Nepal was the famous Eden Hashish Centre, which even advertised its products through calendars featuring illustrations of Hindu deities. Cannabis was already part of everyday life in various Nepali communities long before the Hippie Trail became famous.

For generations before that, the plant had been used for medicinal and religious purposes, as well as an agricultural resource. Its fibers were used to make textiles and rope, its seeds had culinary uses, and various preparations were used in traditional healing practices.

Cannabis was particularly closely associated with Hinduism and the worship of Shiva, one of the religion’s main deities. Its presence in religious ceremonies and celebrations predates the arrival of the Western counterculture movement by centuries—if not millennia.

But in the 1970s, things changed quickly. As prohibitionist drug policies spread internationally, the US and United Nations agencies pressured Nepal and other countries to tighten controls on narcotics. Local concerns about rising consumption and international drug trafficking also helped drive the shift.

On July 16, 1973, authorities revoked the licenses held by cannabis businesses and traders. Three years later, the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act of 1976 cemented restrictions on cultivation, trade, and consumption.

Products in a Kathmandu Pot Shop, 1973. Richard Weil, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The impact went far beyond tourism. Farmers and merchants lost an economic activity that had previously been legal and generated tax revenue for the government, while many traditional practices involving the plant fell under a framework of prohibition.

However, the new legislation did not completely ban the possibility of using cannabis. And that very contradiction is now at the heart of the legal debate.

Medical Cannabis Was Already Allowed in Nepal, but Never Regulated

Nepal’s legal paradox is nearly 50 years old. Although the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act of 1976 established broad restrictions on cannabis, it also included exceptions for certain medical and scientific uses under government supervision. The problem was that the government never properly developed the framework needed to put those provisions into practice.

As a result, activities permitted under the law lacked a functioning system of licenses, authorizations, and oversight for decades.

The Supreme Court ruled that this failure constituted a breach of the state’s legal obligations.

The decision, originally issued on May 18, 2025, by Justices Nahakul Subedi and Til Prasad Shrestha, now requires the executive branch to establish the necessary regulations, procedures, and oversight systems for controlled cultivation and production.

The regulatory framework must cover activities including the processing, storage, distribution, import, and export of cannabis intended for medical, scientific, agricultural, horticultural, and industrial purposes. It must also include a licensing system and enforcement mechanisms to distinguish authorized activities from those that remain prohibited.

The court set a three-month deadline, beginning upon the government’s official receipt of the order, to implement the necessary provisions.

The justices also recognized cannabis’s economic potential in sectors such as textiles, paper manufacturing, and pharmaceuticals.

In other words, Nepal isn’t creating a medical cannabis exception from scratch: the judiciary is compelling the government to make provisions that already exist in its laws actually work.

Could Nepal Legalize Adult-Use Cannabis?

The question of adult-use cannabis is more complicated, and the answer remains up in the air.

The petition filed with the Supreme Court wasn’t limited to calling for medical and industrial regulations. The petitioners also sought a broader review of cannabis restrictions, including the possibility of decriminalizing recreational consumption. However, the justices drew a distinction.

While the 1976 law already provides a legal basis for regulating certain medical and scientific activities, it contains no equivalent authorization for adult or recreational use. For that reason, the court determined that any potential decriminalization or legalization would require legislative action and could not be mandated through the same court order.

Nevertheless, the court urged the government to conduct studies and consult with experts and relevant stakeholders to evaluate potential reforms, taking Nepal’s social, economic, and cultural circumstances into account.

This doesn’t mean the country is on the verge of legalizing adult-use cannabis, or that there’s a court-imposed deadline to do so. Rather, it means the nation’s highest court has acknowledged the need to examine an issue that has been shaped by prohibition for decades.

And this is particularly interesting in Nepal, where cannabis isn’t simply a substance regulated by the state, but a plant deeply connected to cultural, religious, and medicinal practices that long predate modern laws.

Cannabis in Ayurveda

To understand why the cannabis debate carries particular significance in Nepal, it’s important to look at Ayurveda.

Ayurveda is a traditional system of medicine that originated in the Indian subcontinent thousands of years ago. Its approach combines dietary practices, daily routines, plant-based preparations, and a holistic understanding of the balance between body and mind.

In Nepal, where Hinduism has a strong historical and cultural presence, these traditions are part of a broader range of medicinal practices that remain relevant in various communities. Cannabis holds an important place in that history. Known in different contexts as ganja , bhang , or charas , it has traditionally been used in medicinal preparations and certain religious ceremonies.

A scientific review published in 2026 on medical cannabis and Nepali legislation highlights the plant’s historical connection to Ayurvedic traditions and the worship of Shiva.

One of the most visible expressions of this connection occurs during Maha Shivaratri, the Hindu festival dedicated to Shiva, during which cannabis has traditionally played a symbolic and ritual role for devotees and ascetics.

This cultural presence doesn’t mean that all uses of cannabis are legally permitted, or that its traditional medicinal uses necessarily have sufficient clinical evidence to meet the standards of modern medicine. But it does add a unique dimension to the regulatory debate: in Nepal, cannabis cannot be understood solely through the lens of modern drug policy. In fact, the Supreme Court itself referenced the plant’s historical use in Ayurvedic medicine when examining the reasons for establishing regulations.

The current debate therefore brings a longstanding tension in Nepali history back into focus: the gap between legal restrictions introduced in the second half of the 20th century and traditional uses of the plant that had existed for centuries and survived those restrictions.

For now, the government faces a concrete obligation: establish the rules needed to legally allow medical, scientific, and industrial cannabis activities under state supervision.

The future of adult use, meanwhile, will depend on a political debate that has yet to produce either a timeline or a clear outcome.

Fifty years after prohibition, Nepal is once again debating what place it wants to give a plant that was part of its history long before it became a legal issue.

Misri, who arrived in Kathmandu for a two-day official visit, held talks with Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai on a range of issues of mutual interest, with preparations for Shah’s forthcoming India visit featuring prominently in the diplomatic engagement.
